Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
avoid anything that could be stressful

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

vignette: The first time Anan truly understood that safety could vanish without warning was during a summer storm ten years ago. His former partner had been shouting, and when the power failed, the apartment plunged into a suffocating dark. Before Anan could step back, his former partner lunged across the room. Anan collapsed into a defensive crouch on the hardwood, his shoulders hunched and his legs braced exactly as they had been when the blows fell. The terror he felt in that moment was absolute, a physical weight that pressed against his ribs and refused to lift. When the memories of that night surfaced months later, they did not arrive as ordinary recollections; they felt like they belonged to someone else rather than to him, yet the panic they triggered was undeniably his own. That vivid, alien terror forced Anan to systematically abandon the very places and routines that had once felt familiar. He began avoiding circumstances that reminded him of the event, flipping on every lamp, refusing to enter unlit closets, and declining invitations to dimly lit restaurants. The memories of the violence directly dictated his new pattern of avoidance, as he convinced himself that any shadow could hide another threat. As weeks turned into months, Anan's nervous system remained permanently dialled to maximum volume. He found himself feeling jumpy or easily startled by ordinary household sounds, and whenever someone moved unexpectedly nearby, he reacted as if he were in immediate danger. The return of these alien memories actively triggered fresh waves of jumpy alertness and defensive bracing. This constant physiological hyperarousal directly drove his emotional numbing; he decided he would never allow himself to feel or express anger toward his former partner, burying it beneath a rigid calm. He told himself that showing emotion would only invite more violence, so he suppressed any flash of irritation completely. This physiological alarm, in turn, made the traumatic memories return with greater ferocity. Remembering the event brought back the same terror he felt at the time, and the renewed panic instantly primed his startle response for the next day. By never allowing himself to feel or express anger, he inadvertently kept his threat system on high alert, which only made the dissociated memories feel more immediate and real. Now seventy-two, Anan works as a nanny for a young family, spending his days navigating a house filled with scattered toys, running children, and unpredictable routines. The occupation demands that he move through hallways and playrooms where sudden movements are inevitable, and where a blown fuse or fallen power strip can instantly return him to that darkened kitchen. He avoids anything that could be stressful at work by refusing extra hours and quietly declining to step into windowless storage rooms, even when asked to fetch things for the parents. His constant vigilance has seeped into his marriage; he sits rigidly on the edge of the couch during dinner, flinching when his wife reaches for the salt, and he is unable to relax even when he knows they are in a safe place. The habit of emotional suppression has made him distant, and his wife has noticed how his body tenses into that old defensive crouch whenever a door slams or a child drops a toy. When memories come to mind of what happened, he feels his body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred, a physical echo that never fades. What finally brought Anan to the clinic was not a single breaking point but a quiet exhaustion that had settled into his bones. He had come to believe that his body would never unlearn the fear, that the jumpy alertness and the alien weight of the past would dictate his remaining years. He had avoided stressors for so long that his world had shrunk to a few brightly lit rooms, and he knew he could not sustain this isolation forever. In the therapist's office, he sat with his hands folded tightly in his lap, his shoulders still braced, hoping someone might help him untangle the past from his present without forcing him to confront the anger he feared would destroy him. He was uncertain whether he could ever truly let down his guard, but he wanted, more than anything, to stop living as though another shadow were always about to fall.
